Abstract: Humanoid robots are moving from laboratory platforms toward connected fleets that share workspaces, infrastructure, tasks, and knowledge with other robots and humans. As deployments grow, the operation and improvement of each humanoid depend on information exchanged across the network. However, existing research has largely studied humanoids as individual systems. This survey examines networked humanoid intelligence through four functions of information exchange: communication, coordination, collaboration, and social intelligence with human interaction. We first establish the foundations of networked humanoid systems, define the question addressed by each function, and connect them through a common factory scenario. We review the literature along six dimensions: interaction architecture, exchanged information, physical coupling, operating timescale, system scale, and embodiment. We separate results obtained with physical and simulated humanoids from those based on other robotic platforms or disembodied agents, because the latter do not fully capture humanoid-specific constraints such as balance, whole-body motion, contact, and physical interaction. We examine hardware, datasets, and benchmarks, and distinguish risks handled locally from those networking introduces, such as stale information or unsafe knowledge propagation. Finally, we identify open problems in control-aware networking, compact body-centric messages, physically grounded coordination, network- and embodiment-aware knowledge sharing, fleet-level social consistency, and accountable human oversight.

</details>

Abstract: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.

Abstract: Quadrotor interceptors equipped with strapdown cameras offer a low-cost solution for physically countering unauthorized UAVs. However, this configuration inherently couples vehicle maneuvering and camera pointing, creating a conflict between rapid closing and maintaining target visibility. We present interception-oriented spherical-bearing nonlinear model predictive control (ISB-NMPC), which couples spherical-bearing prediction with nonlinear quadrotor dynamics to jointly optimize target-directed closing motion and visibility. An attitude-compensated extended Kalman filter on S^2 estimates target bearing motion, compensates for perception delay, and predicts target bearings to guide scale-adaptive detection. Across 30 paired simulation trials, ISB-NMPC achieves an interception success rate of 86.7%, the highest among the evaluated controllers, with a mean per-trial target-visible time of 99.11%. Outdoor flights demonstrate acquisition of a 30 cm target at approximately 150 m, with interceptor speed reaching 17 m/s in the long-range flight and approximately 14 m/s while pursuing a quadrotor-towed maneuvering target. Abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. Abstract: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.

</details>

Abstract: Grasping is a foundational capability in robotic manipulation. Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis relies on point clouds for metric geometry, yet real-world point observations are often noisy, incomplete, and over-smoothed. RGB images provide object-region, boundary, and appearance cues, yet two bottlenecks limit their effective use in scene representation and local grasp reasoning. We present MMGNet, a Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network that addresses these bottlenecks through hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection and rotational graspness modeling. Hierarchical injection integrates multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation, while the rotational graspness jointly predicts the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before organizing local image-informed features through grasp-shaded grouping. Ablation studies show that these two modules provide complementary gains. MMGNet achieves a mean AP of 60.34 on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense, surpassing all compared methods. Abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.

</details>

Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev's structured, probabilistic decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations, task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates, while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one trainable decision core. Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000 trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance. The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.

</details>

Abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.

</details>

Abstract: Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensor data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine the magnitude, direction, and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and are typically thin, like cables and wires, strain gauges and actuation readings are usually impractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only, thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Abstract: Large vehicles in cluttered environments are often blocked by movable obstacles, motivating mobile robot teams to clear traversable corridors. Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches often abstract obstacle displacements while neglecting robot dimensions, obstacle mass, contact geometry and forces, yielding physically infeasible plans. PushAround is a physics-informed hybrid search that couples geometric connectivity reasoning with short-horizon simulation to construct executable clearing plans. Repeated W-clearance connectivity graph (WCCG) queries expose frontier gaps requiring widening and rank them by estimated downstream costs. The search generates direct or recursive pushing candidates, selecting obstacles, directions, contacts and forces, and admits physics-evaluated candidates. Numerical experiments validate WCCG against standard connectivity checks and demonstrate scaling to denser clutter and teams of up to four robots, with robustness to simulated execution-side physical-parameter mismatch.

Abstract: Dexterous manipulation of rigid objects has reached a level of maturity where grasp stability, control, and planning strategies are successfully applied in industry and logistics. In contrast, manipulating deformable objects (cables, plastic pieces, cloth) remains far more challenging, as rigid-object methods do not account for their additional complexity. This paper identifies semantic failure analysis as a key step toward mature deformable-object manipulation and supports this claim with proof-of-concept experiments. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, where goals are well-defined in terms of criteria such as force balance and slippage, deformable-object manipulation involves a broader variety of failure modes arising from differences in materials, geometry, and behaviour. Typical failures include buckling, plastic deformation, pressure variations, and tearing. These diverse and often hard-to-detect events require distinct corrective strategies, making semantic failure analysis necessary. We define its key components and challenges and present experimental results supporting its potential as a research direction.

Abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.

</details>

Abstract: Existing robot navigation methods primarily focus on isolated tasks, overlooking the need to accumulate knowledge and experience across repeated navigation episodes. Although recent lifelong navigation methods have explored cross-task knowledge accumulation, they mainly focus on scene knowledge while neglecting historical navigation experience and its connection to scene evidence, limiting the ability to reflect on past mistakes and improve future decisions. To address this limitation, this paper presents RetroNav, a training-free self-evolving navigation framework that integrates navigation, memory accumulation, and failure reflection. Specifically, we develop a unified memory system that connects geometric and semantic scene knowledge with historical navigation experience, distinguishing objective observations from task-dependent interpretations. After each navigation attempt, an independent evaluator determines whether a retry is necessary. If so, a Retrospection Agent revisits historical decisions using accumulated scene knowledge and navigation records, generating an evidence-grounded retry brief to guide the next attempt. RetroNav achieves state-of-the-art performance across five navigation benchmarks. Our method will be open-sourced at https://github.com/3dv-casia/RetroNav .

Abstract: Adaptive robot perception systems must balance detector accuracy, inference latency, and energy consumption, particularly when high ambient temperatures cause processors to thermally throttle. We propose Thermal-Headroom Routing (THR), a lightweight model-selection policy that forecasts processor temperature using a closed-form RC thermal model and excludes detector configurations predicted to cross a throttling threshold. We evaluate THR with four YOLO11 configurations across seven real-world perception traces, eight ambient temperatures, and 20 randomized seeds, comparing it with latency-aware routing, fixed-threshold thermostats, duty caps, and a matched-compute-budget control. At ambient temperatures of 45-55 degrees C and a tight inference deadline, THR eliminates throttling in simulation, reduces deadline misses by 3.9-7.5 percentage points, and reduces energy per on-time frame by approximately 12-13% relative to a latency-belief router. A separate experiment using deadline-paced, nonoverlapping frame execution yields miss-rate reductions of 6.2-9.5 percentage points. A tuned thermostat or duty cap can match THR at a fixed operating point; predictive routing is most useful when ambient conditions or calibrated thermal parameters differ from those used to tune static policies. Measurements on an Apple M5 support the single-node heating approximation but do not validate hardware throttling. The results characterize the conditions under which thermal forecasting improves the efficiency and timeliness of resource-constrained robot perception.

</details>

Abstract: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.

This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. Abstract: Accurate localization in GPS-denied and visually degraded environments affected by smoke, dust, or fog remains a critical challenge for autonomous systems. While LiDAR provides high-resolution spatial perception, its performance deteriorates under particulate occlusion. In contrast, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar offers robustness under such conditions but suffers from sparse measurements and outliers. This article presents a resilient decentralized LiDAR Radar Inertial Odometry (LRIO) framework that fuses the complementary strengths of LiDAR, radar, and inertial sensing to achieve robust pose estimation in challenging subterranean environments. At the core of the framework is an Adaptive Residual Thresholding (ART) mechanism that autonomously detects temporal sensor degradation and selectively adjusts the fusion process to minimize unreliable measurements. Building on this, a Robust Error-Tolerant Optimal Information Filter (RETOIF) is employed within a decentralized fusion architecture to integrate LiDAR-inertial and multiple radar-inertial odometry estimates in a fault-aware manner, enhancing resilience to environmental disturbances and intermittent sensor failures. The proposed framework is evaluated using real-world sensor data collected in GPS-denied subterranean tunnels under smoke-free and smoke-degraded conditions. In the smoke-free experiment, the proposed RETOIF framework achieves a root mean square localization error (RMSE) of 2.1733, compared with 2.9929 for the conventional centralized LRIO approach, corresponding to a 27.4\% reduction in RMSE. Experimental results further demonstrate the framework's ability to maintain pose estimation under smoke-induced sensor degradation, highlighting its potential for resilient autonomous navigation and mapping in challenging subterranean environments.

</details>

Abstract: Embodied agents are expected to accomplish real-world goals by deciding for themselves how and when to interact with their surroundings. For many such goals, changing the physical state of the world is the means rather than the end: the agent changes the state of a system through interaction, observes the feedback, and explores until it either achieves the goal itself (e.g., discovering physical laws) or learns what the goal requires; it acts to know. Manipulation benchmarks stop at acting to change, with the target state given; scientific discovery benchmarks evaluate knowing but replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numerical queries. We introduce EmbodiedLab, a benchmark in which a robot must act to know. Quantitative science experiments make this setting controllable: the parameters of the system are resampled for every instance, so the result cannot be known in advance, yet it can be scored exactly. Across 30 experiments in five disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms, the agent receives an objective and the apparatus, chooses its own procedure, and operates a physics-based simulated laboratory, reading the instruments through its cameras. Evaluation checks what the agent came to know, grounded in readings recorded during the episode, as well as the physical state the task requires; every experiment is verified to be solvable. We evaluate six frontier models in their developers' coding agents with native observation and control, with added perception and motion planning, and with manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. With native control, even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; for every agent, most failures arise in interacting with the apparatus, and manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The benchmark and its evaluation code are available at https://github.com/HexaFuture/EmbodiedLab.

</details>

Abstract: While unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed for pipeline inspection, prevailing research predominantly assumes static pipes. In real-world industrial environments, pipes often exhibit dynamic movements, such as vibrations. This imposes more stringent requirements on UAVs' adaptive control and computational efficiency than in static scenarios. Therefore, this paper proposes a servo control framework named VisGeo-PipeTrack, which utilizes geometric constraints to enable UAV tracking of dynamic pipes. To achieve efficient UAV positioning, YOLOv5 is employed to detect labels on the pipe. The positions are derived from visual geometric constraints based on these detected labels to enable precise localization. To address tracking control challenges, a model predictive control based real-time corrected adaptive PID (MPC-RCAPID) controller is proposed. This controller employs the Recursive Least Squares method for real-time model estimation and integrates rolling horizon optimization to dynamically adjust PID parameters. Experiments conducted on both the AirSim simulator and the Tello UAV platform validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework. Simulation comparisons with standard PID, fractional-order PID, adaptive PID, and fuzzy PID demonstrate that MPC-RCAPID achieves the shortest settling time (3.26 s) and the lowest average tracking error (3.52%). In physical experiments on the Tello platform, compared with standard PID control, MPC-RCAPID reduces the average tracking error by 55.52%, 26.72%, and 26.52% across the three test dimensions. These results demonstrate that VisGeo-PipeTrack facilitates efficient autonomous tracking in dynamic pipe environments.

</details>

Abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.

</details>

Abstract: Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model. This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks. Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss-Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.

Abstract: Training robotic manipulation policies in simulation is widely adopted due to safety and cost efficiency; however, tasks involving obstacles remain under-performing and often converge slowly under Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). To address this challenge, we propose a task decomposition framework for DRL that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and robustness in obstacle environments. The TL strategy selectively transfers only the first-layer critic parameters across structurally related tasks, since that layer captures general state--action representations while deeper layers encode reward- and obstacle-specific value geometry; RR decomposes tasks into staged sub-objectives to provide denser optimization signals. Experiments on the PyBullet Panda platform show consistent gains in obstacle settings. On Push with obstacle, our method achieves $0.83 \pm 0.05$, outperforming the strongest baseline (Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), $0.77 \pm 0.06$) by approximately $7.8\%$. On Slide with obstacle, performance reaches $0.95 \pm 0.02$, exceeding Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) ($0.84 \pm 0.06$) by about $11\%$ success rates. In addition to higher final performance, forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to $70\%$ in obstacle tasks, and RR shortens sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from roughly $0.75$M to $0.20$M steps ($\approx73\%$ reduction). The best policy is deployed on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot as a qualitative feasibility demonstration.

Abstract: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.

</details>

We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.

</details>

Abstract: In autonomous driving, robot teleoperation serves as a critical safety fallback mechanism, requiring operators to assume direct control in the event of system failure. While recent research has pivoted toward high-level supervisory control or simulation-based studies, these approaches often fail to capture the physical dynamics and sensory demands of driving a full-scale vehicle. To address this gap, we evaluated the impact of spatial data representation on operator performance using a real car-sized vehicle in a field experiment with $N = 18$ participants. We compared three visualization interfaces: (i) a standard camera feed baseline, with two bird's-eye views (BEV) from (ii) a raw LiDAR point cloud, and (iii) a sensor fusion of LiDAR and camera data streams. Contrary to prior passive observation studies suggesting that sensor-fusion BEV may hinder awareness, our active-control results demonstrate that such representation significantly outperforms the standard LiDAR BEV in perceived usability ($p \leq 0.0001$) and cognitive task load ($p = 0.01$, NASA-TLX score: 34.58/100) while also being significantly better than the Camera-only view ($p = 0.043$). The fused interface also led to statistically significant reductions in task completion time ($p = 0.0461$) and superior usability (SUS: 77.9/100) compared to those of the Camera-only and LiDAR-only views. By synthesizing objective performance data with comprehensive subjective assessments, we demonstrate that BEV fusion maximizes safety margins while minimizing the operator's mental demand. These findings challenge existing teleoperation conventions and provide an empirically validated approach for designing robust remote piloting systems.

</details>

Abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$

Abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot's behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Abstract: Agile quadruped navigation in dynamic environments demands trajectories that are both dynamically feasible and provably collision-free. Most real-time planners achieve tractability through a convex reduction that requires simplified kinematic models, discarding motion that the robot can readily execute, and certify safety only at discretization points, leaving open possible inter-sample collisions with moving obstacles. We present a real-time motion planning framework that retains the fully-actuated $SE(2)$ model of a quadruped, with its anisotropic, heading-coupled velocity bounds, and accepts the resulting nonconvexity. By parameterizing trajectories as composite Bernstein polynomials, we exploit the convex hull property to certify collision avoidance and the input bounds over the entirety of each planning horizon. Solved at online replanning rates, the optimization runs in closed loop, commanding body velocities to the locomotion controller. We validate the approach in simulation against ablations and external baselines, and in hardware experiments on a quadruped navigating among unknown moving obstacles, recovering both lateral and heading-coupled motion that simplified models exclude.

</details>

Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. Abstract: Simulation benchmarks are a useful way to measure progress in robotics; typically they provide success rate as the dominant measure of performance. However, success rate reports only whether a rollout completed the task, hiding by what margin it succeeded, how sensitive the success is to goal parameter changes, requirements it may have violated, and whether success persisted. Signal Temporal Logic (STL) provides a formal language for capturing specifications; it can be used to define requirements, and measure how close a robot behavior is to satisfying or violating them. Using STL monitors in a simulator, however, requires exposing simulator state and mapping it to specification-relevant signals. We present Specola, a tool for evaluating robot behaviors in simulation with respect to STL specifications. Specola provides an interface for writing specifications over simulator signals, and creates and manages the relevant monitors while a policy executes. We provide a Python API and command-line interface for integrating monitoring into existing policy execution loops. We provide an adapter interface for connecting new simulators, and provide adapters for nine simulation environments and benchmarks, including LIBERO, RoboCasa, Isaac Lab, and RoboDojo. We provide case studies that illustrate the nuanced evaluation that Specola enables. Code and adapters are available at https://github.com/specola-eval/specola.

</details>

Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Abstract: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxcé-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io

Abstract: This article investigates the discernibility of topology changes in networked linear time-invariant systems, with particular focus on edge disconnection. We introduce a new notion of discernibility motivated by a limitation of the definition commonly adopted in the literature. In consensus networks, topology changes are inherently indiscernible for all initial conditions belonging to the synchronization subspace. To overcome this issue, we first introduce the notion of dynamical discernibility of a topology change for elementary consensus networks. This notion explicitly disregards the intrinsic indiscernibility associated with states in the consensus subspace. We characterize this property for directed communication graphs and then specialize the resulting conditions to topology changes arising from either the disconnection of an edge or a variation in its weight. We then extend the analysis to networks of homogeneous agents by introducing discernibility modulo synchronization, which factors out the unavoidable indiscernibility associated with synchronized trajectories. We derive a general characterization showing how discernibility depends jointly on the topology change and on the dynamics of the individual agents. Finally, we specialize the analysis to undirected communication graphs and show that, under mild additional assumptions, discernibility modulo synchronization is equivalent to the dynamical discernibility of the corresponding topology change. This establishes a direct connection between the two notions and extends existing results on the discernibility of topology variations in dynamical networks. The resulting characterizations are then further specialized to the case of edge disconnection.

</details>

Abstract: Wireless underground sensor networks (WUSNs) enable in-situ monitoring of subsurface processes and buried assets to deliver substantial social and economic benefits across diverse verticals. However, meter-scale underground monitoring remains challenging since conventional WUSNs place the entire underground device at the target sensing depth, where severe soil-induced attenuation significantly degrades communication reliability and makes wireless energy transfer (WET) inefficient and even impractical. To address this limitation, we propose Terra-Fi, a novel shallow-hub and deep-sensing architecture that decouples the sensing depth from the wireless communication and energy-replenishment depth. In Terra-Fi, a shallow wireless hub is deployed at a depth favorable for communication, WET, and maintenance, while application-specific sensing probes are extended to meter-scale target layers through power-and-signal feeders. On this basis, we first examine the depth limitations of underground communication and WET and compare representative monitoring architectures. Then, we present its system architecture, operation flow, and potential benefits. Through a precision agriculture case study, our numerical results reveal that Terra-Fi establishes more robust wireless connectivity and a longer operational lifetime than conventional fully buried WUSN architectures, particularly at greater sensing depths and higher volumetric water content. Moreover, its performance gain can be enhanced through time allocation and transmission-configuration optimization. Finally, we pinpoint practical challenges and future research directions for deploying Terra-Fi into WUSN systems.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming formulation that concurrently optimizes the placement and scheduling of space-based observers for cislunar SDA. Our work considers three aspects of observer scheduling: sensor tasking, communication, and charging. We utilize a scenario-based approach that generalizes observer placement for unknown targets while applying scheduling constraints to each scenario. However, this problem quickly becomes difficult for commercial solvers to handle as the number of scenarios grows. As an alternative, a column generation approach is employed to introduce well-performing schedules into the problem for each orbital slot. A comparative analysis is performed across multiple instances to evaluate the performance of column generation against that of a commercial solver. A case study is then conducted in which the performance of the observers' placement from the concurrent formulation is tested against a set of validation target sets and compared with the performance of two baselines in which placement and scheduling are performed sequentially.

Abstract: Intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) have advanced learner motivation and personalization in cognitive domains, but extending these gains to psychomotor tasks remains challenging. Existing psychomotor ITSs rely on learner models built before instruction or updated once per module, leaving open how to use real-time assessments of learner cognitive state for finer-grained personalization. Psychomotor learning involves multiple tutoring objectives, including calibrating self-confidence to performance, calibrating workload per the Yerkes-Dodson Law, and driving skill progression toward higher learning stages. How to balance these objectives for learners, and adjust that balance over time, remains open. This study proposes and evaluates an online personalization algorithm that continuously reprioritizes tutoring objectives to match learners' evolving needs. Rather than weighting objectives equally, the actor-critic-inspired algorithm dynamically updates reward weights using recent measures of self-confidence, workload, and performance. These weights inform a multi-input, multi-output cognitive control framework that synthesizes learner-specific tutoring policies via model-based planning. The approach was evaluated in a human-subject study (N = 40) with a 2D quadrotor landing task. Clustering of the learned reward weights revealed distinct prioritization patterns across learners, indicating the algorithm captures heterogeneity in learner needs. Learners whose weights shifted more substantially tended to reach higher final performance, and those whose weights consistently emphasized workload calibration achieved the strongest outcomes. These findings advance online learner modeling and control-based personalization in psychomotor ITSs, showing how adaptive tutoring can better support learning by aligning instructional decisions with learners' evolving cognitive and performance states.

</details>

Abstract: Hybrid dynamical systems flow continuously but jump at discrete events. We show that the more closely a PINN follows a jump, the larger its physics loss must be. We propose hybrid-time PINNs (HT-PINNs), which assign one network to each flow interval of the hybrid time domain and train the networks jointly with the jump times and the unknown parameters. The number of jumps and the sequence of modes are found by enumeration. HT-PINNs recover the number of jumps and the restitution coefficient of a bouncing ball. In a MuJoCo simulation of robotic disassembly, where a robot pulls a press-fitted pin out of a housing through a spring, HT-PINNs find the number of jumps and the sequence of modes, and estimate the static and kinetic friction coefficients with small errors of 0.1% and 1.7%.

Abstract: Learning controllers from trajectories corrupted by process and measurement noise is difficult when the system matrices and the noise covariances are unknown: noisy regressors bias least squares, and model uncertainty cannot be quantified without the noise covariance, which can only be estimated from residuals of the uncertain model. This paper, Part~I of a two-part study, resolves both obstacles with a finite-sample framework that certifies, and iteratively refines, uncertainty sets for the model, the noise in the collected data, and the noise covariance. A closed-loop parametrization based on delayed instrumental variables (IVs) removes the bias and assigns to every candidate model exactly one noise sequence that reproduces the data. Learning this noise breaks the circular dependence: the noise sequences give the covariance estimate directly, models whose noise violates the prior or the statistical certificates are discarded, and the surviving models yield a tighter covariance certificate. Several delayed instruments further tighten the model set and give a certified test of data consistency. We prove finite-sample containment of the true model, noise, and covariance, recursive nesting, and convergence at the IV rate. Part~II uses these certificates for domain-randomized linear quadratic regulator synthesis.

</details>

Abstract: Building on the uncertainty description developed in Part~I, this paper introduces a Fisher-majorized domain-randomized generalized policy iteration framework for data-driven linear quadratic regulator (LQR) synthesis. At each iteration, partial Bellman evaluation over a fixed batch of uncertainty realizations produces a structured Sylvester policy-improvement step. A residual-weighted Fisher curvature controls the policy-induced variation in the stationary covariance and converts the Sylvester model into a certified upper bound on the cost change, thereby guaranteeing descent for every accepted step. A check-and-correct mechanism then certifies stability over the entire uncertainty support, rather than only over the sampled realizations. Consequently, every iterate is robustly stabilizing and monotonically decreases the fixed-batch objective. The Fisher truncation and stability correction become inactive after finitely many times. The objective gap then contracts linearly to a floor determined by the dispersion of the realization-wise Riccati targets and by measurement noise. In the absence of measurement noise, this floor vanishes when the realization-wise targets coincide.

Abstract: Detecting communities, i.e., groups of densely connected nodes, usually requires a central entity that knows the whole network. We study Recursive Neighbor Pruning (RNP), a fully decentralized alternative inspired by social learning. Each agent holds a private opinion but only shows its neighbors a coarse public action, namely its opinion amplified and clipped to a fixed range. Agents repeatedly move their opinion toward the actions of their neighbors and, once opinions settle, drop the links with neighbors whose action has the opposite sign. Repeating this procedure on the remaining network splits it into communities, without any agent knowing the network or the number of communities. We use tools from nonlinear control to characterize this behavior. We show that splitting requires the amplification to exceed a threshold set by how strongly the network is bottlenecked. We also show that a group in which every member has enough of its links inside the group can no longer be split once its members agree, and that a single run separates such groups exactly when started from suitable opinions. Finally, we bound the number of runs and messages. On two standard families of synthetic networks, RNP is as accurate as the best centralized method as long as each node has fewer than about forty percent of its links outside its community, and it fails close to the value predicted by our analysis. It is more accurate than two decentralized competitors below this level, but exchanges many more messages.

</details>

Abstract: Measurement-based parameter estimation of the WECC composite load model (CMLD) commonly relies on voltage replay, where measured voltage is imposed on an isolated CMLD and its parameters are optimized to reproduce measured active and reactive power. However, this open-loop formulation neglects the two-way dynamic interaction between the load and grid, potentially causing large errors when the estimated model is reinserted into dynamic grid simulations. To address this limitation, we propose a closed-loop parameter estimation framework that alternately estimates the CMLD parameters and a five-parameter equivalent network representing the external grid. This framework restores load-grid interaction during estimation and enables voltage, active power, and reactive power to jointly constrain the parameter estimation. Compared with four baseline methods, the proposed approach achieves the highest reinsertion accuracy in both the CMLD benchmark and transmission and distribution (T&D) co-simulation environments. In the T&D case, it reduces active-power, reactive-power, and voltage errors by 73%, 64%, and 62%, respectively. The identified model also maintains improved reinsertion accuracy under disturbances not used for estimation, demonstrating transferability beyond the identification event.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is driving an unprecedented expansion of data centres. Unlike electricity, computation can be moved across the globe through fibre-optic networks, but whether this spatial transfer can bypass constrained grids and accelerate global AI data-centre deployment remains unknown. Here we develop a global framework that places future data-centre capacity in energy-abundant regions and routes computational workloads through fibre-optic networks rather than transmitting electricity. Results show that across multiple data-centre development and climate-policy scenarios, leveraging global data transfer allows new data centres to be sited where these conditions are favourable, lowering construction costs by 44-47% and carbon emissions by 38%. By treating the global fibre-optic network as an energy-system asset, it avoids 34-67 GW of high-voltage transmission capacity, comparable in magnitude to Italy's national peak electricity demand. Crucially, this methodology could bring more than 95% of connection-delayed data centres online in 2030, with Canada, the Nordic countries and the Arabian Peninsula emerging as preferred locations for data-centre development. Our findings establish computational mobility as an alternative to energy-system expansion, informing the coordinated global development of energy and artificial-intelligence infrastructure.

Abstract: The carbon footprint of generative-AI inference depends not only on hardware efficiency and electricity supply, but also on whether the selected model is appropriate for the task. A frontier model may expend unnecessary computation on a routine request, whereas an under-capable model may increase energy use through failure, retries, extended reasoning and escalation. However, a standardized evaluation framework that accounts for task-specific capability requirements and the carbon emissions associated with successful task remains lacking. In this Perspective, we argue for a capability-constrained carbon labeling framework that shifts environmental assessment from carbon intensity per inference towards the expected carbon emissions per successfully completed task at the required capability level. Under this framework, models would first be assessed against task-specific capability requirements, and only models capable of meeting those requirements would be compared on their expected energy use and operational carbon emissions. By linking service quality to carbon cost, this approach could enable more informed matching of the right model to the right task, offering a demand-side pathway to reducing emissions associated with generative-AI token use. Realizing this vision will require standardized capability-based service assessments, comprehensive energy accounting and transparent carbon disclosures.

Abstract: We consider decentralized stochastic nonconvex optimization over directed networks. Push--Pull provides an efficient decentralized optimization framework for such networks, but in the stochastic setting, gradient variance can slow its convergence and complicate the analysis of linear speedup. Motivated by this observation, we incorporate recursive momentum into stochastic Push--Pull for variance reduction, yielding the accelerated stochastic Push--Pull (ASPP) algorithm. Under mean-squared smoothness, we prove that ASPP improves the convergence rate of stochastic Push--Pull and achieves asymptotic linear speedup with respect to the number of agents. To further reduce communication, we develop LASPP, a local-update variant of ASPP that allows each agent to perform multiple local updates between communication rounds. We show that LASPP achieves an additional asymptotic linear speedup with respect to the number of local steps. With a suitable number of local steps, LASPP reduces communication complexity while maintaining the same stochastic gradient complexity as ASPP. Numerical experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

Abstract: This paper proposes and analyzes a dual-measurement frequency-droop (DMFD) controller for meshed MVDC networks. Using only two local DC measurements, bus-voltage deviation and a filtered DC-port current or power deviation, the controller enables grid-forming operation at both AC and DC ports across the mesh. Although the DMFD regulates neither the DC voltage nor the DC current directly and acts only on the terminal frequency, it is shown that AC-side synchronization closes an effective DC droop at every synchronized terminal, so that the steady operating point of the mesh exists and is unique. Constant frequency deviations at a terminal and single-terminal islanding enter the same DC equations as equivalent current offsets, with the island frequency fixed by the island power balance, allowing node voltages and branch currents to be obtained from one linear system. The steady-state model yields design-use envelopes to map the droop ratios and the net DC-injection levels into bounds on DC-voltage deviation and terminal currents. A small-signal dynamic model is developed and used to generate eigenvalue loci and damping-ratio charts that guide controller-gain selection. Averaged EMT simulations on a four-terminal ring corroborate the analysis: in regimes where PLL-based grid-following control is known to lose damping, the DMFD controller maintains stable operation and follows the predicted steady-state characteristics.

Abstract: The security region (SR) specifies a joint feasible region in the operational space involving various installations within the power system. It enables dynamic allocation of capacity among these energy units, thereby unlocking additional grid potential for power delivery and mitigating congestion. By constructing a convex hull from a set of vertices to form a polytope, the SR can be effectively represented with an acceptable accuracy loss. However, the SR computation inevitably generates many low-quality vertices, which contribute little to the overall hypervolume and can be discarded. By introducing SR compression, the SR data size can be reduced, which in turn facilitates the memory-efficient computation of SR and time-efficient solution of SR-related optimization problems. Accordingly, this paper proposes a vertex pruning approach that mixes local and backward search policies to achieve effective SR compression. In particular, the backward search strategy allows previously pruned vertices to be recycled when they are re-identified as critical. Subsequently, we incorporate this approach to enhance computational efficiency in the aforementioned applications. Numerical validations are conducted on two realistic medium-voltage Dutch grid cases. The results demonstrate at most 1.65% hypervolume loss with over 96.0\% SR data size reduction after applying the proposed compression approach. Empowered by this compression, the 8-dimensional (8D) SR becomes computationally tractable. Moreover, in relevant grid-aware computation challenges, the solving time can be reduced by at least 52.9% with at most an 1.36% optimality loss. All above validate both the efficacy and values of the proposed SR compression approach.

</details>

Abstract: Video token compression must control both temporal coverage and task relevance, but sequential stages can conflict: a content-driven allocation stage may be overwritten by a global ranking that removes entire temporal positions. We identify this as an allocation conflict and propose TeQCo, a training-free framework that resolves it through temporal quota consistency. TeQCo allocates candidate capacity from first-order changes in normalized frame representations and aggregates all tokens within each frame into a compact candidate set. Candidates are then scored by prior-corrected task attention and selected within integer frame quotas inherited from the first-stage counts. Content variation determines temporal capacity; question relevance determines which candidates fill it. This design guarantees an exact token budget and a per-frame coverage floor whenever feasible. On the 2,700-question Video-MME benchmark with Qwen3-VL-8B, TeQCo achieves 68.52% accuracy at 510 ms TTFT, a 32.9% TTFT reduction with a 1.00-percentage-point accuracy decrease.

Abstract: Video vision-language models process thousands of visual tokens before producing an answer. Reducing these tokens early saves computation, but also determines which evidence reaches the language model. We introduce ContextTom, a training-free framework that separates the timing of temporal and spatial compression. Its central idea is to compress time before vision encoding while preserving spatial coverage through early multimodal processing. A fixed-budget temporal partition produces representative medoid anchors, supplemented with bounded local detail from neighboring observations. The anchors retain their complete spatial grids through a short decoder prefix, allowing question tokens to access the visual evidence and completing Qwen3-VL's multi-level visual injections. ContextTom then selects spatial representatives using query attention and agreement across visual feature levels, and continues directly from their computed states. This schedule reduces vision computation and later decoder workload while reusing the prefix. On Qwen3-VL-8B, ContextTom achieves 76.22% accuracy on Video-MME Short with a mean time-to-first-token (TTFT) of 123.5 ms, yielding a 2.77x speedup over full-input inference. These reset-created priors do not reproduce complete, naturally evolved exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) histories. Abstract: Low-count imaging arises when limited illumination or dose yields only a few detected particles in microscopy, such as photons or electrons, causing measurements to be dominated by signal-dependent Poisson shot noise. Supervised denoisers typically require paired clean and noisy observations, whereas many self-supervised approaches exploit spatial or temporal redundancy without directly estimating the underlying particle-arrival process. We introduce PARM, a self-supervised denoising framework based on particle-arrival-rate matching. By modeling particle accumulation over exposure as a Poisson counting process, PARM identifies the conditional particle-arrival-rate field with the posterior mean of the latent clean rate. Poisson thinning then splits each observation into complementary lower-exposure views that provide self-supervised rate targets for one another. In implementation, the network estimates the normalized spatial allocation of the conditional rate, while the observed total count determines its global particle mass. Experiments on synthetic data, natural-video sequences corrupted with Poisson noise, and real low-dose electron microscopy demonstrate leading or competitive performance while effectively preserving fine structures. PARM therefore provides a statistically grounded approach to low-count image denoising when clean references are unavailable.

</details>

The registration establishes spatial correspondence between OCT tissue morphology and LS fluorescence signals throughout development, enabling integrated longitudinal analysis of structural and molecular changes in living embryos.

Abstract: Crack propagation provides richer information than static crack observations for evaluating structural conditions of concrete infrastructure and planning maintenance strategies. Unlike static crack detection, which can now be largely automated using computer vision, vision-based crack tracking is a coupled cross-view and cross-time problem: the same physical crack must retain its identity as camera viewpoints change, while newly developed growth must be distinguished from existing crack segments in a unified reference view. Existing segmentation and 3D reconstruction methods can recover crack masks or scene geometry, but they do not preserve crack identity across views or quantify temporal extension. To address this gap, this study formulates crack growth monitoring as a cross-view and cross-time crack-instance tracking task and proposes a geometry-assisted, morphology-aware framework. The framework first uses image-based geometric registration to align observations from different viewpoints into a shared structural reference, then applies morphology-aware instantiation to assign physically interpretable crack identities, and finally performs temporal mapping in the unified view to distinguish newly developed growth from existing crack segments. To enable evaluation, a temporally annotated dataset was established and used, covering three representative cracking scenarios: single dominant crack propagation, mixed-mode branching, and multiple-crack interaction, with pixel-level masks and cross-time instance labels. Experimental results show that the proposed framework can establish loose cross-view identity correspondence under changing viewpoints, while strict spatial overlap and growth localization remain limited by early micro-crack segmentability and projection drift, highlighting directions for future crack-monitoring research.

</details>

We propose Semantic-Guided Adaptive Latent-Frequency Modulation (SG-AFM), which uses a semantic structural prior to guide attenuation of encoder latents. Abstract: Diffusion models are powerful priors for inverse problems, including accelerated MRI. However, modeling the distribution of high-resolution images requires large networks with high computational cost. We propose a posterior sampling framework that uses cascaded diffusion models as multiscale priors. Conditioned on a coarse image, the distribution of fine-scale detail is local and well conditioned, and it can therefore be captured by a small network. Similarly, a small unconditional network is sufficient to represent low-resolution images, and it is used to recover the coarse image from the k-space center. This estimate then conditions the high-resolution prior, which is combined with all measurements to recover the final image. Both priors are trained on images alone, so they apply to any sampling pattern, and data consistency remains linear at every scale. In multi-coil brain MRI, the proposed method improves on the best single-scale diffusion baseline by 4-6 dB in PSNR at 15x acceleration, while each of its separately trained networks is about 10x smaller. The gain grows as the problem becomes more ill-posed, and ablations show that it arises from informative low-resolution conditioning.

</details>

Abstract: Accurate segmentation of thyroid nodules in ultrasound images is essential for clinical diagnosis yet remains challenging due to boundary ambiguity, speckle noise, and complex geometric variability. Existing methods often fail to reconcile global semantic understanding with precise local boundary delineation, leading to errors in irregular cases. To address this, we propose SDFA-Net, a framework built on semantic-aware deformable feature alignment that explicitly decouples the learning of robust global semantics and detailed local geometry. Our approach integrates three main components: a clustered linear context aggregation module for efficient long-range dependency modeling, an affinity-driven token modulation mechanism using dynamic prototypes to suppress background interference, and a cascaded spatially-aligned feature fusion strategy that achieves sub-pixel geometric alignment across multiple resolution stages. By filtering and aligning multi-scale features, SDFA-Net ensures robust fusion that is both semantically meaningful and geometrically accurate. We validate our method through extensive experiments on three public thyroid ultrasound datasets, TN3K, TUCC, and DDTI, where it demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. The proposed framework offers a generalizable solution for precise medical image segmentation in boundary-ambiguous scenarios.

Multi-seed variance analysis demonstrated that the DenseNet201+ViT backbone yielded the lowest deviation (0.59) and highest stability, making it the most reliable architecture for real-world clinical integration. Conclusions: To overcome diagnostic challenges, future research must focus on multimodal architectures that combine 3D volumetric extraction with clinical data.

Abstract: Quick Response (QR) code deblurring must ultimately recover the encoded payload, yet how accurately the underlying camera motion must be estimated remains an open question. To address this question, we formulate motion-blurred QR recovery within a unified mathematical framework of identifiability and systematically measure the decoding tolerance to perturbations in motion length, direction, rotation or scaling centre, and speed profile. These controlled experiments reveal three structural laws: 1) parameter tolerances shrink rapidly as blur amplitude grows and are tightest under uniform speed, whereas accelerating motion is substantially more forgiving; 2) length tolerance can differ markedly between underestimation and overestimation; 3) errors that are individually benign interact strongly and prevent decoding when combined. Guided by these findings, we propose a grey-box recovery pipeline in which two compact networks predict an initial corner trajectory, followed by tolerance-guided candidate search, alternating image-and-path fitting, and regularised linear inversion. On a new benchmark of 955 handheld motion-blurred photographs captured across four phone models and four motion categories, our method recovers the exact payload on 93.1% of the images, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned deblurring network at 83.6% and reducing the decoding error rate by 58.0%.

</details>

Errors were concentrated near water boundaries, and high predictive entropy identified many, but not all, erroneous pixels. These results support a specific role for compact pretrained models: lower measured computational demand with competitive accuracy, rather than consistent superiority. Event-dependent performance, shared hyperparameter selection, and the distinction between observed water and newly inundated land delimit the conclusions.

Abstract: Multimodal medical AI requires a common visual interface for encoding heterogeneous imaging evidence for patient condition modeling. However, existing medical visual tokenizers are often tied to a specific dimension and imaging modality, forcing multimodal systems to rely on fragmented and poorly reusable representations. We introduce MedVTok, a general-purpose visual tokenizer that maps 2D images and 3D volumes from diverse imaging modalities into a unified token space. Building such a tokenizer poses two key challenges: preserving anatomical structure across dimensions and capturing clinical semantics across modalities. To this end, MedVTok introduces (i) slice differential regularization, which explicitly models inter-slice anatomical coherence missing in previous per-pixel/per-voxel supervision, and (ii) multi-expert representation alignment, which integrates knowledge from multiple medical expert encoders while retaining modality-specific complementary knowledge. Trained on 28M images and 70K volumes across 9 imaging modalities, MedVTok supports classification, retrieval, segmentation, synthesis, visual question answering, and medical report generation through a single tokenizer. Across 24 benchmarks, MedVTok achieves state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating a scalable token interface that unifies medical image dimension, modality, and task usage.
